items.title: The Falling Phone
items.question: A phone's accelerometer reads 9.8 m/s^2 while resting on a table. The phone then falls inside a vacuum chamber. Ignoring air resistance, what should it read during the fall?
choices: About 9.8 m/s^2 downward
Nearly zero until impact
About 19.6 m/s^2 downward
An increasing value as speed rises
items.correctAnswer: Nearly zero until impact
items.correctExplanation: Correct. An accelerometer measures proper acceleration from support forces, not coordinate acceleration; in free fall, phone and sensor mass follow the same local geodesic.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The reading is nearly zero until impact because gravity accelerates the entire instrument together. The table produced the earlier reading by continually pushing the phone away from its free-fall path.
items.lessonContent:
Accelerometers measure departure from free motion rather than velocity or coordinate acceleration.
A support can create a reading even while an object remains at fixed coordinates.
Freely moving test bodies define local inertial motion in general relativity.
Impact produces a large reading because contact abruptly changes that motion.
Share this: open a phone sensor app and compare its reading flat, tilted, and gently tossed onto a cushion.

items.title: Two Sealed Rooms
items.question: One small sealed lab rests on a planet where tidal effects are undetectably tiny. An identical lab accelerates uniformly through empty space. Which experiment performed entirely inside can identify the planetary lab?
choices: Timing how fast a dropped ball reaches the floor
Measuring the force needed to hold a mass still
Watching a pendulum hang toward the floor
No local experiment under those ideal conditions
items.correctAnswer: No local experiment under those ideal conditions
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. In a sufficiently small region, uniform acceleration and a uniform gravitational environment produce the same local outcomes; only nonlocal information or detectable tidal variation can separate them.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, no local experiment under those ideal conditions can distinguish the rooms. Drops, scales, and pendulums respond to the same effective downward direction in both, which is the operational content of the equivalence principle.
items.lessonContent:
Equivalence is a statement about experiments confined to a sufficiently small spacetime region.
Local means both spatially small and brief enough that field variation is negligible.
Mechanical, optical, and clock experiments must agree under the same idealization.
Information from outside the laboratory can break a comparison that local data cannot.
Share this: ask a friend what a sealed room would need to measure before claiming it knows where it is.

items.title: Converging Drops
items.question: Two balls are released side by side in a very wide, freely falling shaft above Earth. Sensitive tracking shows their separation slowly shrinks as both descend. What does that observation reveal?
choices: A tidal effect that cannot be removed across the whole shaft
Air pressure pushing both balls toward the centerline
A failure of equal free-fall acceleration
A support force acting despite the shaft's fall
items.correctAnswer: A tidal effect that cannot be removed across the whole shaft
items.correctExplanation: Right. Radial free-fall paths point toward Earth's center, so neighboring geodesics converge; their relative acceleration is a measurable signature of spacetime curvature.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! It is a tidal effect that cannot be removed across the whole shaft. Each ball is locally weightless, yet comparing separated trajectories exposes variation in the gravitational field that no single freely falling frame erases everywhere.
items.lessonContent:
Curvature is detected by comparing nearby free trajectories, not by inspecting only one.
Tidal effects describe relative stretching or squeezing between separated test bodies.
A local inertial frame removes uniform first-order effects at one event.
Field gradients survive that choice and become important over larger regions.
Share this: draw two arrows toward Earth's center at separated locations and extend them until their convergence is obvious.

items.title: Laser Across Deck
items.question: A rocket accelerates upward through empty space while a laser fires horizontally across its cabin. Relative to marks painted on the cabin wall, where does the beam arrive compared with its launch height?
choices: Higher, because acceleration adds energy to light
At the same height, because light ignores acceleration
Lower, because the cabin rises while light crosses
Randomly displaced by the observer's motion
items.correctAnswer: Lower, because the cabin rises while light crosses
items.correctExplanation: Correct. In an inertial view the light travels straight while the accelerating cabin rises beneath it, so cabin coordinates describe a downward-curving path, matching the local gravitational prediction.
items.incorrectExplanation: The beam arrives lower because the cabin rises while light crosses. Light does not need a downward force in the inertial description; equivalence requires the same apparent sag in a laboratory supported in a gravitational field.
items.lessonContent:
Accelerating coordinates can make straight inertial paths appear curved.
Equivalence applies to light experiments as well as falling material objects.
Coordinate descriptions may differ while the recorded meeting event remains invariant.
A geometric account avoids treating photons as tiny projectiles with rest mass.
Share this: sketch the same beam once against empty space and once against the rising cabin walls.

items.title: Rocket Clock Ladder
items.question: Identical clocks are fixed at the nose and tail of a long rocket undergoing steady proper acceleration, with the nose in the effective 'up' direction. After accounting for signal travel time, how do their rates compare?
choices: The tail clock runs faster because it began accelerating first
The nose clock runs faster than the tail clock
Both rates remain identical because the rocket is rigid
The comparison depends only on the clocks' brands
items.correctAnswer: The nose clock runs faster than the tail clock
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. The accelerating frame has a position-dependent clock rate: the clock higher in the effective field accumulates more proper time, reproducing gravitational time dilation locally.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The nose clock runs faster than the tail clock. Signals exchanged while the receiver changes velocity reveal the same rate gradient that stationary clocks exhibit at different gravitational potentials.
items.lessonContent:
Equivalence connects clock-rate gradients in supported frames with those in accelerating frames.
Comparing remote clocks requires correcting for changing signal travel times.
Proper time is the duration recorded along each clock's own worldline.
Rigid acceleration in relativity cannot assign identical proper acceleration to every point.
Share this: place two clock icons on a rocket drawing and predict which accumulates more proper time before checking.

items.title: Erasing the Field
items.question: A researcher chooses freely falling coordinates so a dropped particle has no gravitational acceleration at one event. What has the coordinate choice physically eliminated?
choices: All curvature throughout the surrounding region
Every measurable tidal effect for all time
The planet's mass-energy source
The connection terms at that event, not curvature generally
items.correctAnswer: The connection terms at that event, not curvature generally
items.correctExplanation: Right. Local inertial coordinates can make the connection vanish at one event, but curvature depends on derivatives and combinations that remain detectable through nearby relative motion.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the connection terms at that event, not curvature generally. Coordinates can remove a local appearance of force, but they cannot erase invariant tidal relationships over a finite neighborhood.
items.lessonContent:
Coordinate-dependent quantities can vanish by choosing a convenient freely moving frame.
Invariant curvature is encoded in how such local frames fail to fit together across a region.
A zero value at one point need not imply zero spatial or temporal derivatives.
Physical claims should be tied to measurements that survive relabeling.
Share this: challenge one statement that confuses choosing coordinates with changing the underlying system.

items.title: Orbiting Scale Test
items.question: An astronaut in a circular orbit carries a perfect accelerometer, while mission control reports a large inward coordinate acceleration. How can both readings be correct?
choices: The astronaut follows free motion while coordinates curve around Earth
The accelerometer is shielded from gravity by the spacecraft
Centrifugal force cancels gravity inside the sensor only
Orbital speed converts gravitational force into mass
items.correctAnswer: The astronaut follows free motion while coordinates curve around Earth
items.correctExplanation: Correct. The astronaut's worldline is geodesic and has zero proper acceleration, while Earth-centered coordinates assign that curved path an inward coordinate acceleration.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the astronaut follows free motion while coordinates curve around Earth. No shielding or exact force cancellation is required; proper acceleration and coordinate acceleration are different observables.
items.lessonContent:
Proper acceleration is what a carried accelerometer records along a worldline.
Coordinate acceleration depends on the reference coordinates used to describe that path.
Free orbital motion can be curved on a map while remaining force-free locally.
Separating these meanings prevents apparent contradictions between instruments and tracking data.
Share this: ask someone whether a zero accelerometer reading guarantees a straight line on every map.

items.title: Grounded Accelerometer
items.question: A precision accelerometer sits motionless on Earth's surface and points upward. In general-relativistic terms, why does it register about 1 g although its height is constant?
choices: Earth's rotation alone creates the full reading
Gravity pulls only the sensor's internal proof mass
The ground forces it away from its natural free-fall path
Its fixed coordinates guarantee zero proper acceleration
items.correctAnswer: The ground forces it away from its natural free-fall path
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. The surface supplies an upward contact force that prevents geodesic motion, and the accelerometer records that proper acceleration even at constant height.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite. The ground forces it away from its natural free-fall path. Being stationary in Earth-fixed coordinates is not inertial rest; the support continuously bends the instrument's worldline away from free motion.
items.lessonContent:
Weight is associated with support forces rather than with free motion itself.
A worldline can stay at fixed spatial coordinates and still possess proper acceleration.
Contact pressure is locally measurable without looking outside the laboratory.
Free-fall and supported rest exchange the everyday roles of 'accelerating' and 'stationary.'
Share this: compare what a bathroom scale reports in a parked lift, a rising lift, and a falling lift.

items.title: Charged Drop Pair
items.question: A charged and an uncharged sphere are released together in a falling laboratory, but a strong external electric field acts only on the charged sphere. They separate. Does this observation by itself violate gravitational equivalence?
choices: Yes, because all released bodies must share every trajectory
No, because a composition-dependent nongravitational force acts
Yes, because electric charge changes gravitational mass
No, because equivalence applies only to neutral planets
items.correctAnswer: No, because a composition-dependent nongravitational force acts
items.correctExplanation: Right. Universal gravitational free fall is tested only after controlling other forces; the electric field supplies a known, charge-dependent acceleration unrelated to gravitational universality.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! No violation follows because a composition-dependent nongravitational force acts. Equivalence does not claim differently charged objects respond identically when an electromagnetic field is deliberately added.
items.lessonContent:
Universality tests compare bodies after accounting for every relevant nongravitational interaction.
Charge, magnetism, buoyancy, drag, and thermal forces can imitate differential falling.
A clean null test changes composition while suppressing known confounders.
A principle should not be blamed for effects outside the conditions it specifies.
Share this: list three forces an experimenter must control before comparing two falling materials.

items.title: Quiet Horizon Crossing
items.question: A large spacecraft coasts across the event horizon of a supermassive black hole. Its cabin is small enough that tidal effects are negligible there. What does a sealed accelerometer register at the crossing?
choices: An infinite outward acceleration
A sudden reversal from down to up
Exactly the black hole's surface gravity
No special spike; it remains near zero
items.correctAnswer: No special spike; it remains near zero
items.correctExplanation: Correct. A freely falling horizon crossing is locally ordinary when curvature across the cabin is mild; the horizon is a global causal boundary, not a material surface that strikes the craft.
items.incorrectExplanation: The reading shows no special spike; it remains near zero. Hovering near a horizon would require enormous proper acceleration, but coasting through it is locally free motion rather than collision with a wall.
items.lessonContent:
Local instruments need not detect a boundary defined by the future escape of light.
Free fall and hovering are physically different worldlines near compact objects.
Curvature strength at a horizon depends on the central object's mass.
Global causal structure can matter even when one crossing event looks locally uneventful.
Share this: explain to someone why a map boundary need not behave like a physical membrane.

items.title: Two Horizon Sizes
items.question: Two astronauts cross the horizons of black holes with very different masses. Which astronaut can experience weaker head-to-foot tidal stress exactly at the horizon?
choices: The one crossing the more massive black hole
The one crossing the less massive black hole
Both, because every horizon has identical curvature
Neither, because tidal stress is infinite at any horizon
items.correctAnswer: The one crossing the more massive black hole
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. A more massive black hole has a much larger horizon radius and weaker curvature at that radius, so a large traveler can cross before severe tidal gradients develop.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the one crossing the more massive black hole can experience weaker tidal stress. Horizon status does not set one universal local curvature; small black holes have much steeper gradients at their horizons.
items.lessonContent:
Tidal stress depends on how rapidly a gravitational field varies across an object's size.
A boundary's causal importance does not fix its local curvature magnitude.
Scaling a compact object's mass also scales the radius of its horizon.
Comparing gradients, not merely field labels, predicts stretching and compression.
Share this: contrast a steep small whirlpool with a broad gentle one as a gradient analogy.

items.title: Falling Sphere Swarm
items.question: A small spherical cloud of freely falling beads approaches a compact mass. No bead feels a support force. Which deformation most directly expresses geodesic deviation?
choices: Uniform shrinking in every direction
Rigid translation with no internal change
Radial stretching paired with sideways squeezing
Random heating caused by vacuum friction
items.correctAnswer: Radial stretching paired with sideways squeezing
items.correctExplanation: Right. Neighboring radial paths separate while neighboring transverse paths converge, turning the initially spherical swarm into an elongated shape even though each bead is locally weightless.
items.incorrectExplanation: The deformation is radial stretching paired with sideways squeezing. Curvature acts through relative acceleration between neighboring geodesics, not through drag or an equal compression in all directions.
items.lessonContent:
Geodesic deviation predicts relative motion among neighboring freely moving test bodies.
Tidal geometry can stretch along one axis while compressing along others.
Each member may read zero proper acceleration even as the group's shape changes.
Extended collections reveal information unavailable to a single pointlike observer.
Share this: draw a circle of dots and deform it using inward side arrows and outward radial arrows.

items.title: Flat Yet Heavy
items.question: An accelerating laboratory in otherwise flat spacetime has floor scales, hanging pendulums, and position-dependent clock rates. Which further result would show its apparent gravitational field is not caused by spacetime curvature?
choices: Dropped objects reach the floor
A complete tidal measurement finds zero curvature
The floor scale reports a nonzero weight
Light appears to bend in laboratory coordinates
items.correctAnswer: A complete tidal measurement finds zero curvature
items.correctExplanation: Correct. Acceleration can reproduce uniform local gravitational phenomena in flat spacetime, but an invariant tidal survey distinguishes coordinate gravity from genuine curvature over a region.
items.incorrectExplanation: The decisive result is that a complete tidal measurement finds zero curvature. Drops, weights, clock gradients, and apparent light bending all occur in accelerating coordinates and therefore do not establish curved spacetime by themselves.
items.lessonContent:
Inertial effects can imitate a uniform gravitational field inside an accelerating frame.
Curvature requires invariant relative-motion measurements across neighboring trajectories.
A coordinate force may be useful without representing a new physical field source.
Local equivalence does not make all extended gravitational situations globally identical.
Share this: sort four familiar effects into those one point can measure and those requiring spatial separation.

items.title: Spinning Habitat Test
items.question: A rotating space habitat produces floor weight that resembles gravity. Which cabin experiment can distinguish it from a small nonrotating room supported in an approximately uniform gravitational field?
choices: Weighing one stationary object
Dropping an object straight toward the floor
Timing a pendulum's ordinary period
Launching objects sideways and detecting Coriolis deflection
items.correctAnswer: Launching objects sideways and detecting Coriolis deflection
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Rotation creates velocity-dependent Coriolis effects detectable inside the habitat, so rotational artificial gravity is not locally equivalent to simple linear acceleration for all motions.
items.incorrectExplanation: The distinguishing test is launching objects sideways and detecting Coriolis deflection. Static weight alone can look gravitational, but rotation leaves direction- and velocity-dependent signatures beyond a uniform downward acceleration.
items.lessonContent:
Rotation is absolute enough to reveal itself through local inertial effects.
Coriolis deflection depends on an object's velocity relative to the rotating frame.
Centrifugal strength also changes with distance from the rotation axis.
Artificial weight can match one gravitational feature without matching every experiment.
Share this: predict which way a tossed ball curves inside a clockwise rotating room.

items.title: Cable Cut Reading
items.question: A person stands on a scale in a lift held motionless above Earth. The cable snaps, and the lift enters ideal free fall. What happens to the scale reading before any impact?
choices: It falls to nearly zero because person and scale share free fall
It doubles because Earth accelerates both downward
It stays unchanged because gravitational mass is unchanged
It becomes negative because the lift moves downward
items.correctAnswer: It falls to nearly zero because person and scale share free fall
items.correctExplanation: Right. A scale measures contact force; once the lift, person, and scale follow neighboring free-fall paths together, that support force nearly disappears.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! It falls to nearly zero because person and scale share free fall. The person's mass and Earth's gravity remain, but weight as a contact reading vanishes until tides or impact create relative force.
items.lessonContent:
Scales report normal force rather than an object's invariant mass.
Support force disappears when an observer and instrument enter the same free motion.
Changing velocity direction does not make a force reading negative.
Operational definitions clarify why mass can remain while apparent weight changes.
Share this: state what a scale actually measures before using the word weight in one conversation.

items.title: Engine-Off Course
items.question: A probe near a star switches off its engine and follows a curved orbit. Which description best fits general relativity from the probe's local perspective?
choices: A hidden force pulls it off its natural straight path
Its inertia shuts down until the engine restarts
It follows the straightest available spacetime path
Its mass continually converts into orbital speed
items.correctAnswer: It follows the straightest available spacetime path
items.correctExplanation: Correct. With no thrust, the probe follows a geodesic: locally inertial motion whose projection into space can look like a curved orbit because spacetime geometry is curved.
items.incorrectExplanation: The probe follows the straightest available spacetime path. Calling the spatial orbit curved does not imply a local force; the full spacetime trajectory is the free-motion path selected by the geometry.
items.lessonContent:
A geodesic generalizes straight inertial motion to curved spacetime.
Spatial pictures omit the time dimension and can make free paths look force-bent.
Engines and supports create departures from geodesic motion that instruments can feel.
Geometry predicts trajectories without requiring gravity to act as an ordinary push.
Share this: trace a route on a globe and compare its flat-map curve with its surface geodesic.

items.title: Half a Prediction
items.question: A calculation treats starlight as fast Newtonian particles responding only to a gravitational potential and predicts half the observed deflection near a star. What did that approximation omit?
choices: Photons losing rest mass as they travel
The contribution of spatial curvature to the null path
Atmospheric refraction at the star's surface
Quantum collapse caused by the telescope
items.correctAnswer: The contribution of spatial curvature to the null path
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. A potential-like time-curvature argument captures only part of general relativity's result; spatial geometry contributes the other part to the light ray's null geodesic.
items.incorrectExplanation: The missing piece is the contribution of spatial curvature to the null path. Light has no rest mass to lose, and the factor-of-two discrepancy arises from incomplete spacetime geometry rather than telescope or atmospheric effects.
items.lessonContent:
Relativistic predictions use the geometry of both space and time.
A Newtonian analogy can capture one limit while omitting equally real geometric terms.
Light follows null trajectories determined by the full spacetime metric.
Agreement in order of magnitude does not guarantee a model contains the whole mechanism.
Share this: find one scientific analogy and ask explicitly which part of the full theory it leaves out.

items.title: Self-Energy Fall
items.question: Lunar laser ranging checks whether Earth and Moon fall toward the Sun at slightly different rates because Earth contains more gravitational binding energy. Which principle is this especially testing?
choices: Conservation of electric charge
The uncertainty principle for massive bodies
Only equality of ordinary material composition
Strong equivalence including gravitational self-energy
items.correctAnswer: Strong equivalence including gravitational self-energy
items.correctExplanation: Right. Comparing bodies with different fractions of gravitational binding energy probes whether gravity itself falls universally, a stronger demand than ordinary composition tests with laboratory materials.
items.incorrectExplanation: The test targets strong equivalence including gravitational self-energy. Earth and Moon differ not only chemically but also in how much of their mass-energy comes from their own gravity, allowing orbital polarization to expose a violation.
items.lessonContent:
Several equivalence principles make related but differently strong claims.
Laboratory composition tests mainly compare nongravitational forms of internal energy.
Self-gravitating astronomical bodies extend the question to gravitational binding energy.
Long-baseline orbital measurements can amplify tiny differential accelerations.
Share this: explain why comparing two planets can test a stronger claim than dropping two laboratory samples.

items.title: Balance of Materials
items.question: A torsion balance compares two materials as Earth falls around the Sun. If their ratios of passive gravitational mass to inertial mass differed, what signal would appear?
choices: A composition-dependent twist synchronized with the Sun's direction
An equal twist for both samples with no daily pattern
A universal change in the speed of light
A loss of mass whenever the balance rotates
items.correctAnswer: A composition-dependent twist synchronized with the Sun's direction
items.correctExplanation: Correct. Unequal gravitational-to-inertial mass ratios would give the samples different solar accelerations, producing a differential torque whose orientation tracks the external field.
items.incorrectExplanation: The expected signal is a composition-dependent twist synchronized with the Sun's direction. A common acceleration largely cancels in the differential instrument; only unequal response between the materials produces the sought torque.
items.lessonContent:
Differential instruments reject effects shared equally by two test bodies.
Torsion fibers convert tiny horizontal force differences into measurable angular shifts.
Changing material composition tests whether internal constitution affects free response.
A predicted time or direction signature helps separate signal from laboratory drift.
Share this: identify one common-mode disturbance that a paired measurement could cancel.

items.title: Twin Mass Gradiometer
items.question: Inside an orbiting satellite, two free test masses each have accelerometers reading zero, yet their separation oscillates slightly along the orbit. What should engineers infer?
choices: The accelerometers disprove the separation data
One mass must be secretly supported
Relative free motion is measuring the local gravity gradient
The masses alternate between having positive and negative inertia
items.correctAnswer: Relative free motion is measuring the local gravity gradient
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Individual zero proper acceleration is compatible with changing separation; a gradiometer measures geodesic deviation and therefore tidal curvature rather than ordinary support force.
items.incorrectExplanation: Relative free motion is measuring the local gravity gradient. The two instruments answer different questions: each accelerometer tests its own support-free path, while their separation tests how nearby free paths converge or diverge.
items.lessonContent:
A gravity gradiometer compares nearby free trajectories instead of measuring one absolute pull.
Common spacecraft acceleration can be rejected while differential motion remains.
Tidal signals vary with orbital position and instrument orientation.
Multiple valid instruments can disagree numerically because they measure different quantities.
Share this: ask what each sensor measures before treating two different readings as a contradiction.

items.title: Oversized Laboratory
items.question: A freely falling laboratory is expanded from one metre to hundreds of kilometres while its instruments become more precise. Which assumption behind treating it as an inertial frame eventually fails?
choices: Free fall works only for microscopic objects
Light ceases to have a constant local speed
Gravity varies negligibly across the laboratory
The laboratory must lose all internal pressure
items.correctAnswer: Gravity varies negligibly across the laboratory
items.correctExplanation: Right. Equivalence supplies a local inertial approximation, but an enormous lab spans enough spacetime for gradients to produce measurable relative accelerations and clock-rate differences.
items.incorrectExplanation: The failed assumption is that gravity varies negligibly across the laboratory. Free fall remains valid for each small part, but no single frame makes an extended, curved region behave inertially everywhere.
items.lessonContent:
Local approximations depend on a scale set by measurement precision and field gradients.
Making an experiment larger can reveal effects hidden in a smaller version.
Curved regions can be tiled with local inertial frames that do not merge into one global frame.
An idealization should always be paired with the regime where its neglected terms stay small.
Share this: name one everyday approximation that fails when the distance or duration becomes large enough.

items.title: Released in Flight
items.question: In a rocket accelerating upward through empty space, an astronaut releases a wrench. In an external inertial frame the wrench then coasts. Why does it hit the cabin floor?
choices: The accelerating floor catches up to the coasting wrench
The wrench acquires gravitational charge when released
The rocket's exhaust attracts the wrench downward
Release removes the wrench's upward inertia
items.correctAnswer: The accelerating floor catches up to the coasting wrench
items.correctExplanation: Correct. Once released, the wrench retains its instantaneous velocity while the rocket continues accelerating, so the floor overtakes it; rocket occupants describe the same event as downward fall.
items.incorrectExplanation: The accelerating floor catches up to the coasting wrench. No new downward interaction appears at release; the apparent field is a consequence of using the rocket's accelerating coordinates.
items.lessonContent:
One event can have a force-free inertial description and an apparent-force accelerating description.
Release removes contact force without erasing an object's existing velocity.
Observers agree on where worldlines meet even when they assign different coordinate accelerations.
Switching frames should not introduce an invented physical interaction.
Share this: draw floor and wrench positions at three successive times in an outside frame.

items.title: Drifting Constants
items.question: Two identical freely falling laboratories perform the same nongravitational atomic experiment at different places and epochs. After standard relativistic corrections, they obtain systematically different dimensionless constants. Which foundational claim would that challenge?
choices: Only the universality of material free fall
Only conservation of angular momentum
The existence of tidal spacetime curvature
Local position invariance within Einstein equivalence
items.correctAnswer: Local position invariance within Einstein equivalence
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Local position invariance requires outcomes of nongravitational experiments to be independent of where and when a freely falling laboratory performs them.
items.incorrectExplanation: The challenged claim is local position invariance within Einstein equivalence. Differential falling concerns trajectories, whereas a reproducible change in a dimensionless atomic result would make local nongravitational physics depend on spacetime location.
items.lessonContent:
Einstein equivalence combines more than the universality of falling test bodies.
Local position invariance demands that nongravitational laws not depend on place or epoch.
Dimensionless constants avoid ambiguities caused merely by changing measurement units.
Clock networks and precision spectroscopy can search for tiny violations.
Share this: explain why a changing dimensionless ratio is more meaningful than saying one dimensional constant changed.

items.title: Turning Free Lab
items.question: A compact freely falling lab rotates its apparatus through different orientations while moving through the same event. If a nongravitational interference experiment's result depended on absolute orientation or constant lab velocity, what would be violated?
choices: Local Lorentz invariance
Conservation of gravitational binding energy
The definition of an event horizon
Only Newton's inverse-square approximation
items.correctAnswer: Local Lorentz invariance
items.correctExplanation: Right. Local Lorentz invariance says nongravitational experiments in a local inertial frame do not reveal an absolute uniform velocity or preferred spatial orientation.
items.incorrectExplanation: The violated principle would be local Lorentz invariance. A repeatable orientation- or boost-dependent local result would identify a preferred frame, contradicting a central component of Einstein equivalence.
items.lessonContent:
Local Lorentz symmetry denies preferred inertial directions and uniform velocities in local physics.
Rotating an apparatus is a standard way to search for anisotropy.
Comparisons over time can exploit Earth's changing orientation and motion.
A local symmetry test is conceptually distinct from measuring tidal gravity.
Share this: identify what pattern a preferred direction would leave as Earth turns during one day.

items.title: Antimatter Drop
items.question: Neutral antihydrogen released in Earth's field is observed to accelerate downward. Which conclusion is scientifically justified from that result alone?
choices: Antimatter has no gravitational response
All strong-equivalence tests are now complete
A simple universal upward-antigravity model is disfavored
Antihydrogen must fall at exactly g with unlimited precision
items.correctAnswer: A simple universal upward-antigravity model is disfavored
items.correctExplanation: Correct. Downward acceleration rules against the popular claim that antimatter universally falls upward, while finite experimental precision leaves room for testing smaller differences in magnitude.
items.incorrectExplanation: The justified conclusion is that a simple universal upward-antigravity model is disfavored. One measurement does not prove exact equality to arbitrary precision or settle every stronger equivalence claim.
items.lessonContent:
Experiments constrain specific alternatives within stated uncertainties rather than proving exact equality forever.
Neutral composite antimatter reduces electromagnetic disturbances that would swamp a gravity test.
Direction and magnitude are separate questions with different evidential demands.
A broad principle can survive while precision tests continue narrowing possible violations.
Share this: rephrase one absolute science headline as the narrower model constraint the data actually support.
